title: The river passes
hook: Confucius stands by a river and says it flows on like this, day and night (Analects 9.16)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mencius's sprout: the jolt of care at a child near a well, there before any reason. Your line was the seed is there.

Have you ever stood on a bridge and watched the water go under? It's oddly hard to walk away from. The water you're looking at is gone before you've finished looking, and yet the river stays exactly where it is. Kids stare at it. Old people stare at it. Nobody has to explain why. In China, long ago, a teacher stood by a stream and said one short sentence. Readers still argue about what he meant.
screen: `WATCHING WATER FROM A BRIDGE.` → `GONE, AND STILL THERE.` → `ONE SENTENCE BY A RIVER.`

segments.voice: The teacher is Confucius, and the sentence is in the Analects, the collection of his sayings that, tradition says, his students gathered. In James Legge's old translation, it reads: "The Master standing by a stream, said, 'It passes on just like this, not ceasing day or night!'" That's the whole passage. No explanation, no moral. And because he didn't explain, readers hear two very different things in it. Some hear a sigh: time running away like water, day and night, and us getting older on the bank. Tradition remembers Confucius as a teacher who spent long years hoping a ruler would put his teaching to use; heard that way, it's gentle grief about time. Others hear encouragement. The river doesn't rest on its good days or quit on its bad ones. It keeps going, and over years it cuts through rock. Mencius, yesterday's teacher, praised water that comes from a real spring, because it flows on day and night and fills every hollow before moving on. Some later Confucian readers heard in the river the ceaseless working of the world itself. You don't have to choose; maybe both are true at once. Time does pass, and the way to meet passing time is to keep flowing with it, a little each day. In Greece, Plato reports the philosopher Heraclitus saying you can't step into the same river twice. Two thinkers, far apart, both watching water.
screen: `CONFUCIUS AT THE STREAM.` · `A SIGH ABOUT PASSING TIME.` · `OR: KEEP FLOWING, LIKE WATER.` · `MAYBE BOTH AT ONCE.` · then, large: `DAY AND NIGHT.`

segments.voice: If you're near a river, a fountain, rain, or a tap you can run slowly, watch it; if not, pour a glass and watch the surface settle, or picture a stream you've known. Watch the water arrive and leave without trying to hold any of it. Notice your breath doing the same, in and out, never the same breath twice: just like this.
Confucius. His one sentence at the stream: it goes on like this, day and night. A sigh, or a push, or both.
Your line: day and night. The river keeps going, a little at a time. Day seventy-nine, done.

howItsDone: The line from the Analects is often quoted in Chinese when people speak of passing time, and readers take it as a lament, a call to steady effort, or both.

fork.setup: you're standing with Confucius by a stream. he watches the water, then speaks. what does he say?
options: a river teaches us to rule a kingdom
it passes on like this, not ceasing day or night
let us cross before it rises
fork.reveal: it passes on just like this, not ceasing day or night. that's all he says, and people still debate whether it's a sigh or a push.

notes: Legge's 1861 Analects IX.16 quoted: confirm exact wording and punctuation ('It passes on just like this, not ceasing day or night!').
Mencius 4B.18 (water from a spring flowing day and night, filling hollows): paraphrased; confirm reference.
Heraclitus's river saying is paraphrased and reaches us through Plato's Cratylus; its exact form is debated. Named briefly as a neighbor, not blended.
Chinese 逝者如斯夫，不舍晝夜 and rough pronunciation: confirm.
